title: What Are Your Hands Saying to People
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay is a close study of hand gestures as a leadership communication tool, arguing that hands broadcast intention and expectation as fast as facial expressions do. It contrasts the pointed finger -- almost always an accusation, demand, or reprimand -- with the open palm, which functions as an invitation across dozens of everyday contexts: waving, hand-raising, cheering, slowing someone down, quieting a room, or signaling confusion. The piece closes with a specific practical tactic: using an open, slightly raised palm in a meeting to draw the floor toward yourself without interrupting.
points: Hands broadcast intention and expectation as quickly as facial expressions and eye contact do.
A pointed finger is nearly always experienced as an accusation, demand, or reprimand, and is considered rude in some cultures.
The open palm functions broadly as an invitation -- used in waving, hand-raising, cheering, calming, and quieting gestures.
Presenters often bring palms together as if holding an idea in the air between their hands.
A specific tactic: raising an open palm slightly toward the center of a meeting table reliably draws the floor to you without interrupting.
quotes: A pointed finger is almost always an accusation or a demand for emphasis.
While pointed fingers convey a great deal to others, it is the open palm that commands the most attention.
We use our palms to encourage or restrain the movement of others.
Open palms carry the meaning of an invitation or request in a way others can't miss.
If the person speaking doesn't ask what you want to add, others will quickly turn to you, give you their attention, and wait for you to say something.
